title: Do You Ever Feel Like Your Doctor Hates You?
description: There’s one phrase we learned in medical school that I absolutely hate: “If you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras.” The idea is simple: the most common explanation is usually the correct diagnosis. That works great if you’re a horse. But if you’re a zebra, it sucks. Because when you don’t fit the usual pattern, you can get dismissed or misdiagnosed. And if you’re misdiagnosed, you can get mistreated. Unfortunately, I have a knack for being a zebra. But this thing is: I know some of you reading this are zebras, too. Maybe you’ve experienced symptoms your doctor couldn’t explain. Maybe you’ve received conflicting medical advice. Or maybe you’ve walked out of an appointment feeling confused, dismissed, or wondering whether there’s something important about your health that everyone is missing. I’ve been there. More than once. And through my own experiences navigating unusual medical conditions, I’ve learned something that I wish every patient understood: You have an enormous amount of power in solving your own health problems. And, there’s a way to do this without becoming your doctor’s worst nightmare. But first, let me tell you why I have a particular affinity for zebras. My First Zebra Experience When I was 18, for example, I developed osteoporosis . It wasn’t diagnosed until I was 20, and even then, I was given an explanation that didn’t make sense to me: relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S). Effectively, I was told I wasn’t eating enough energy to support my activity. Even to my incompletely formed brain, that seemed like an unlikely explanation.

title: A Masterclass on Building Stronger Bones
description: Here’s a not-so-fun fact: I used to have osteoporosis. Now, if you know even a little medicine, you might be skeptical. I’m a 30-year-old man who generally reports being healthy. So, the idea that I had osteoporosis sounds extreme. I was diagnosed around age 20 after an unusual series of events. What made the situation so strange is that I had never had any bone problems as a child. My first fracture occurred when I was 18 years old while training for the Boston Marathon. In fact, I was the youngest qualifier for the 2014 Boston Marathon. A short time before the race, however, my tibia broke. (I still ended up crutching the marathon , but that’s a different story.) What was peculiar is what happened afterward. I couldn’t recover. Over the next several years, I developed more and more fractures—first in my legs, then my pelvis, and eventually even my vertebrae. When I finally underwent a bone density scan, the results were shocking: my bone density was in the bottom 1% or less for my age. This was particularly startling because just a few years earlier I had run more than 3,000 miles in a year without so much as a bone twinge. What’s more, there was no obvious explanation. I had a healthy BMI. My testosterone levels were normal. I ate well. I consumed plenty of protein. My vitamin D levels were normal. There was essentially nothing in my bloodwork to suggest I should have the bones of an 80-year-old woman. But I did. *Nick note: The rabbit hole this sent me down ultimately became my first first-author paper : it turns out I have an extraordinarily rare genetic mutation affecting how my bones respond to mechanical loading. In my case, excessive high-impact loading from marathon training was probably breaking down my bones.

title: Rejuvenate Your Body's Anti-Cancer Defenses
description: Somewhere in your body right now, a cell has started down the path toward cancer, and your immune system is finding it and shutting it down before it can ever become a tumor. The problem is that defense system declines as you age. This is, in fact, one of the primary reasons cancer rates increase with age. Not just because you accumulate genetic mutations, but because precancerous cells can escape your body’s natural defenses. But where does this process start to go wrong? One of the immune system’s key command centers is the thymus. It’s a small organ you probably never think about and sits behind your breastbone. And the thymus slowly decays with age, but at different rates in different people. And here’s where things start to get interesting. According to new research published in one of the world’s top science journals, Nature : Humans with faster thymus aging get cancer at higher rates. Conversely, people with unusually young thymuses appear protected from cancer. In one study of over 23,000 adults, those with the healthiest thymuses had a 36% lower rate of lung cancer than those with the more deteriorated thymuses. So here’s the question: If your anti-cancer defenses erode as you age, can you rejuvenate them? In this letter, I’ll show you: How your anti-cancer defenses actually work Why they fade with age Specific peptides I’d actually consider Where caution is warranted. I’m not going to hand you a cure for cancer.
